author: OCEANVIN10
summary: OCEAN highlighted the Memento 3 preprint. Its authors report that a fixed language model revises an external rulebook and executable world model; on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, they report clearing every level with fewer actions than the human baseline. These are author-reported results on the public set.
whyItMatters: A new ARC-AGI-3 research lead for the edition desk. The paper provides a concrete mechanism and results, but the public tutorial set cannot establish private-game performance.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize announced a new 2026 ARC-AGI-2 Kaggle high of 88.06% by Tufa Labs and said a $150,000 bonus would be split among teams scoring above 85%.
whyItMatters: A public-board threshold announcement and major standings lead; the post does not establish a final private score.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize announced Yi-Chia Chen at 59.17% on the 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Kaggle board, taking the lead over Tufa Labs.
whyItMatters: A new public-board leader is the strongest ARC-3 standings lead; verify the current board before an edition.

author: crysis44k
summary: In Japanese, fshindo (@crysis44k) reported reaching the ARC-AGI-2 medal range after substantial effort. The Kaggle profile ffsscf directly links to this X account, and current dated rosters list ffsscf on the separate fshindo teams in ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3. The rank/medal statement belongs to the post’s observation time, not the present board.
whyItMatters: A verified competitor reaction can now be connected to ARC-2 team 17019785, while keeping the author’s posting-time medal claim distinct from current provisional standings.

author: cunkpyber
summary: PunkCyber tells the ARC Daily Digest that 復活の混テキスト is their team. The exact Japanese name matches entries on the current ARC-3 and ARC-2 boards; these have separate competition team IDs.
whyItMatters: A competitor checked in with the paper and supplied a direct team identification. It supports a friendly shout-out; the reply does not identify their individual Kaggle handle or establish who produced a submission.

author: crysis44k
summary: Posting in Japanese, fshindo said the ARC-AGI-3 competition had taught them a great deal about agent harnesses and called contests a valuable learning opportunity. The post links the current Kaggle competition.
whyItMatters: A first-person ARC-3 engineering account, now connected through the direct Kaggle profile link to team 16992721. It is an attributed experience, not a claimed cause of any score.

author: mikeknoop
summary: Mike Knoop said the same thing is happening with ARC-AGI-3 while quoting Pedro Domingos’s comment that models are absorbing harness behavior. The quoted post links Harness Learning Enables Generalizable Test-Time Adaptation. Knoop gives no named team, method, score or ARC experiment. The linked paper trains a proposer to revise executable harness code using feedback; its reported evaluations cover reasoning and multi-hop question answering, so the ARC-3 observation remains Knoop’s attributed comment.
whyItMatters: Fresh ARC co-founder reaction for reporting on how models and harnesses divide the work. Useful research context, with no new verified Kaggle result or evidence that harnesses disappear.

author: Fei2411
summary: FeiZ reported a one-level ls20 ARC-AGI-3 comparison: a DS Bot cleared that level within 81 steps, while a DeepSeek Harness exhausted 110 steps without clearing it. This is the author’s own small test, not a Kaggle standing or verified benchmark result.
whyItMatters: Recent ARC-AGI-3 community experiment; the author explicitly says one level proves little.

author: masspeakss
summary: masspeaks reacted in Japanese to Tufa Labs exceeding 85% on ARC-AGI-2, calling the result impressive. The public board independently shows Tufa Labs at 88.06% in the afternoon snapshot.
whyItMatters: Respectful reaction from a current ARC-AGI-2 mover to the leader.

author: masspeakss
summary: In a Japanese post, masspeaks said careful preparation had paid off and expected a high gold-band cutoff. This is the contestant’s reaction; the post alone does not establish the exact score or method.
whyItMatters: Context from the ARC-AGI-2 public-board mover; compare any score or rank with the board brief.

author: tufalabs
summary: In a reply to Mike Knoop’s ARC-AGI-2 bonus-threshold post, Tufa Labs said it had not set out to solve ARC-AGI-2, started by accident, and plans to share more after the deadline. This is the team’s account, not an independently established history.
whyItMatters: First-person context from the ARC-AGI-2 public-board leader; no method or final result is disclosed.

author: JFPuget
summary: Puget asked ARC Prize whether the 85% bonus threshold refers to the public or private leaderboard; no organizer answer was visible in the checked thread.
whyItMatters: Flags a reporting question; avoid presenting the public score as the final prize result.

author: mikeknoop
summary: Knoop said ARC-AGI-2 remains much harder than ARC-AGI-1 and that eventual open solutions will be useful to study, while quoting his earlier reaction to Tufa Labs crossing the public Kaggle bonus threshold.
whyItMatters: Organizer context about the contest; his forward-looking statement is not a released solution or final award.

author: mikeknoop
summary: Knoop said the 85% Grand Prize bonus threshold had been reached on Kaggle and called 2026 the final ARC-AGI-2 Kaggle year.
whyItMatters: Provides organizer context for the Tufa Labs result; his expectation about future open artifacts is not yet a release.

author: fchollet
summary: Chollet reacted to ARC Prize’s Tufa Labs ARC-2 announcement by saying Kaggle scores are getting very good.
whyItMatters: A founder reaction adds a measured voice to the organizer’s score announcement.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize announced Stephen Wolfram as a keynote speaker for its 2026 Research Summit.
whyItMatters: A current event-program lead for the meeting digest.

author: SimonOuellette6
summary: Ouellette released an ARC-AGI-3-style training-data framework with 429 playable games, solvers and demonstration generators; he said 37 games still lacked solvers. The linked repository says it combines augmented public ARC demos and other game sources.
whyItMatters: A concrete research resource; its author describes training material, not a measured Kaggle-score gain or coverage of private games.

author: JFPuget
summary: Jean-François Puget warns that setting temperature to zero does not guarantee fully deterministic LLM inference. The post quotes a claim that temperature zero always produces the same answer. In a later reply he says the hiring wording should not be taken too seriously and was intended to draw attention to the topic.
whyItMatters: Older catch-up lead for reporting on reproducibility and run-to-run variation. This is Puget’s general inference comment, not a measurement explaining any ARC leaderboard result. Preserve the clarification when using the hiring line.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize published verified Grok 4.7 scores: 1.8% on ARC-AGI-3 with its standard harness, 10.0% with a provider adapter, and 61.4% on ARC-AGI-2.
whyItMatters: The harness distinction matters when comparing model scores; the post reports organizer verification.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize published verified DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scores of 72.9% on ARC-AGI-2 and 94.5% on ARC-AGI-1, with stated per-task costs.
whyItMatters: A dated organizer model verification relevant to ARC-2 comparisons.
